text.content: 1. Intro

rich_text.plain_text: 1. Intro

text.content: The module project asks you to design and build a redesigned agent architecture for a business problem of your choice. Across four sprints you produced a set of deliverables that build on each other: the architecture decision brief that names the pattern, the multi-agent design diagram that shows how the agents relate, the memory and state specification that describes what the system knows and what it forgets, and the integration work on the Flowise canvas that turns those decisions into something that runs.

text.content: Sprint 1: Architecture decision. Read your chosen business case. Apply the four-question framework to decide single-agent or multi-agent. Name the pattern. Write a one-page architecture decision brief covering the six sections (Decision, Pattern, Inputs and outputs, The three pillars, Rejected alternative, Conditions for revisiting).

rich_text.plain_text: Sprint 1: Architecture decision. Read your chosen business case. Apply the four-question framework to decide single-agent or multi-agent. Name the pattern. Write a one-page architecture decision brief covering the six sections (Decision, Pattern, Inputs and outputs, The three pillars, Rejected alternative, Conditions for revisiting).

text.content: Sprint 2: Multi-agent design. Produce a design diagram of your agent architecture — every agent named, information flow shown, routing decision points marked, information boundaries called out, at least one fallback path. Write a design rationale covering diagnosis and justification, agent roles, information boundary, and fallback strategy. Note the rejected alternative if applicable.

rich_text.plain_text: Sprint 2: Multi-agent design. Produce a design diagram of your agent architecture — every agent named, information flow shown, routing decision points marked, information boundaries called out, at least one fallback path. Write a design rationale covering diagnosis and justification, agent roles, information boundary, and fallback strategy. Note the rejected alternative if applicable.

text.content: Sprint 3: Memory and state architecture. Produce the four-section specification: memory boundary map (shared vs private vs conditional, with persistence scope), what must not persist (with the category and prevention strategy for each item), state recovery design (failure scenario, safe state, and specific recovery mechanism), and failure isolation (which agents may write to which state keys, and under what conditions).

rich_text.plain_text: Sprint 3: Memory and state architecture. Produce the four-section specification: memory boundary map (shared vs private vs conditional, with persistence scope), what must not persist (with the category and prevention strategy for each item), state recovery design (failure scenario, safe state, and specific recovery mechanism), and failure isolation (which agents may write to which state keys, and under what conditions).

text.content: Sprint 4: Integration and testing. Implement the design on the Flowise canvas: stage the archetype, enforce memory boundaries, wire up state handoff and recovery, and add the specific safeguards you designed for the failure modes. Run the test set (baseline, boundary, and architecture-specific tests). Refine until each safeguard holds under the tests it was designed for. Export the canvas.

text.content: Minutes 0–1: Context and canvas. Name your domain and business problem in one sentence. Name your archetype in one sentence. Then run the first query live (the common path) and let the execution trace play. While it runs, narrate briefly: which agent is classifying, which specialist is routing to, what is being written to Flow State. The context and archetype sentences should take fifteen seconds; the rest is the live demonstration.

text.content: Minutes 1–2: Architecture and design decisions. Walk through the system diagram. Cover the three defense areas in order; architecture choice, multi-agent design, memory and state. text.content: Architecture coherence
Do the four sprint decisions fit together as a unified design, or do they look like independent exercises that were never reconciled with each other?

text.content: Decision justification
Is each major decision grounded in a specific property of the business problem and domain, or are reasons stated at the level of general principle ("multi-agent is more scalable")?

text.content: Failure handling
Can the learner describe what the system does when something goes wrong — a specialist agent failing, a Classifier producing malformed output, a state key holding a stale value?
